prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps) implements Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), airspace users/operators, aircraft, pilots, controllers, traffic managers and automation participate across National Airspace System (NAS) Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations, including Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS).
FAA/users negotiate assigned closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current-state-to-destination, respecting user constraints. Aircraft must comply within performance/situation-dependent tolerances; aircraft share predicted intent. Controllers retain separation/conflict-avoidance responsibility; routine IFR self-separation is not assumed. Controllers use automation to issue closed trajectories proactively, minimizing voice vectors. Publish changes to affected users, aircraft and FAA automation; consider downstream effects.
NAS Constraint Service publishes static/dynamic constraints; traffic management automation converts traffic management initiatives (TMIs) into traceable flight-specific constraints. Negotiating controllers subsume D-side responsibilities; traffic management coordinators (TMCs) support traffic flow management (TFM). Automation coordinates multisector changes.
Near-term deployment uses automation upgrades/System Wide Information Management (SWIM) extensions and mixed equipage. Structured airspace persists; low/medium-density regions permit more direct routing. Participating equipped aircraft negotiate trajectories and receive fewer interventions.
Far-term assumes widespread Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2). All aircraft digitally receive assigned trajectories and fly with known accuracy; Flight Management System (FMS) loading may be automatic or manual. Voice remains for immediate action/feedback. Electronic flight bags (EFBs) gain reliable high-speed ground connectivity, enabling capabilities outside legacy FMS. Required Time of Arrival (RTA) FMS supports one active RTA; controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) supports clearances/intent.
Traffic Collision Avoidance System/Airborne Collision Avoidance System (TCAS/ACAS) evolves through UAS detect-and-avoid and Advanced Interval Management (A-IM). All IFR aircraft gain coordinated multi-aircraft tactical avoidance, sending planned maneuvers to ground automation via broadband: MBT’s final safety layer.
Ground Delay Programs (GDPs)/Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) shift toward Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at constrained resources rather than departure-time control.

New part:
U0076: The time horizon over which TBFM is applied will expand further into the en route environment, and TBFM will be used to address airspace constraints as well as airport capacity constraints.  Use of generic miles-in-trail (MIT) restrictions (i.e., the same restriction across many aircraft) will be eliminated.
U0077: When metering is not required, aircraft will be spaced for safety and efficiency using either time-based management or A-IM.  MBT facilitates a transition to time-based separation standards.
U0078: Whether the NAS uses distance-based or time-based separation requirements, or a combination of both, to define minimum separation standards, is inconsequential to MBT.
U0079: MBT is able to function for any type of separation requirements.  Aircraft capability to meet TOAC constraints is described using a Required Time Performance (RTP) metric that serves as a complement to existing standards used to describe Required Navigation Performance (RNP).
U0080: An aircraft’s time-based performance is denoted by RTP-Y, where Y is a variable that describes the 95% confidence interval of the expected crossing time error distribution, in seconds, regardless of its shape.
U0081: In an MBT environment, all aircraft will be certified to operate at some RTP level, including aircraft that are not equipped with automation systems that include RTA functionality.  Airspace users’ flight operations centers will develop advanced capabilities to fully participate in MBT.
U0082: Software applications and private service providers will enable non- airline flights to fully participate in MBT.  The NAS will accommodate new aircraft classes, including on-demand travel, personal mobility, UAS, space vehicle launch and return operations, airships, and loitering operations (e.g., to provide communication or ground surveillance services).
U0083: Many of these newer, emerging users are expected to have the necessary capabilities to be fully compliant with MBT. 1.6 Document Scope 1.6.1 Surface Operations This ConOps document focuses on the airborne phases of flight.
U0084: However, MBT is applicable to all phases of flight.
U0085: Although nothing in the MBT concept precludes including a surface trajectory as part of the aircraft’s 4DT, defining the surface trajectory and the aircraft following it would require new ground and aircraft automation capabilities, distinct from those required for airborne MBT trajectories.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
